video_title: PaperTrade Attracted $140M, Then Changed the Rules. Was It a Bait and Switch?
gist: Delphi's Jason Pagalatis dissects PaperTrade, a HyperEVM 'on-chain bucket shop' offering 1,000x BTC/ETH leverage against a house pool, which drew ~$140M in pre-deposits before retroactively scrapping planned PAPER token transferability over oracle-manipulation risk via Hyperliquid prices. He calls it a bait-and-switch rather than a rug, notes staking revenue fell ~93% in a day as farmers left, and argues tokens only work when attached to real businesses like Hyperliquid.

insights.claim: PaperTrade is a house-backed (not order-book) leveraged exchange on HyperEVM offering up to 1,000x leverage on BTC and ETH only, where every trade is taken against a single house pool (Martingale LP), enabling zero funding, zero fees and zero slippage because orders never reach the real market.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: The 'no fees/no slippage' pitch is structural to a counterparty-to-house model, not efficiency; the LP bears all trader PnL risk.
insights.quote: the positions are taken against the house, right? Uh against the house single pool, which I believe they called uh kind of funny funnily is Martingale LP

insights.claim: The Martingale LP started at $0 and is funded entirely by losing traders' margin; when the pool is depleted, winning traders' payouts enter a queue until enough other traders lose money to pay them.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Winners face counterparty/solvency risk: profits are not guaranteed liquid, a hidden tail risk for any participant.
insights.quote: you can't actually get your profits until other people lose enough money to then start paying out the queue again

insights.claim: Losing traders minted PAPER as a rebate (initially ~100 PAPER per $1 USDC lost, with a richer mint rate for the first ~$2M of losses), which could be staked for USDC yield from platform trading activity; winners pay an asymmetric haircut, receiving roughly 88-90%+ of gains, copied from Rollbit.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: The early-loss bonus curve explicitly rewarded racing to lose money, front-loading pool capital from farmers rather than organic users.
insights.quote: the incentive was to be earlier to lose your money, so you would get a higher amount of paper

insights.claim: The PaperTrade team itself likened its model to late-1800s/early-1900s bucket shops, where the house takes the other side of bets on an asset without trading the underlying.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Historical analog signals the regulatory and counterparty profile: this is a casino product, best valued like a gambling house, not an exchange.

insights.claim: 1,000x leverage is gambling, not trading: a 10 basis point move in Bitcoin, which can happen for any reason, is enough to liquidate a position.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Demand for such products is degen entertainment demand; durable volume depends on gambling appetite, not trader PMF.
insights.quote: 500 x trading isn't trading, it's gambling

insights.claim: PaperTrade timed its launch to October 10th to exploit the narrative of the prior year's October 10th liquidation event (Binance issues, cross-venue ADL), pitching that liquidated traders at least get a rebate.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Narrative-timed launches can pull large deposits quickly; investors should separate narrative-driven inflows from product demand.

insights.claim: Crypto Twitter pre-deposited about $140M USDC into PaperTrade before its October 10th launch, and roughly $57M had been paid to staked PAPER holders from trader losses during the first week or so.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Shows how quickly airdrop/farm-driven capital can concentrate in a new HyperEVM protocol, and the scale of losses funneled to stakers.

insights.claim: PaperTrade briefly flipped NASDAQ's daily notional traded volume on one day during its launch week.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin
insights.so_what: Headline notional volume at 1,000x leverage is massively inflated relative to margin; treat such comparisons as marketing, not liquidity.

insights.claim: HyperEVM lacked the throughput to handle PaperTrade's high-frequency speculative closes, creating queues to close positions so that traders using 1,000x leverage could be liquidated before their close order executed.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: HyperEVM capacity is a real constraint for latency-sensitive apps on the Hyperliquid ecosystem; a negative signal for building high-frequency products there.
insights.quote: hyper EVM isn't exactly a super high throughput chain

insights.claim: Because PaperTrade prices off Hyperliquid's mid-price feed, a trader can push BTC or ETH on Hyperliquid's real order book by even sub-1% briefly and profit massively from highly levered PaperTrade positions; this happened on launch day with someone placing $5-20M market orders on the ETH perp while short on PaperTrade.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Any house-pool exchange using an external oracle is exposed to cross-venue manipulation proportional to its leverage and pool size.
insights.quote: You had somebody putting in these, you know, five or 10, 15, 20 million dollar market orders pushing the price around

insights.claim: The PaperTrade team manually locked the manipulating trader's positions so they could not be closed and resolved it privately, showing the 'fully on-chain' protocol is controlled by a multisig (reported by The Defiant as a 2-of-3) with full admin power.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: 'Fully on-chain' does not mean decentralized; admin keys can freeze positions, a key governance risk for depositors.
insights.quote: it's not like fully decentralized, right? Like it's still a multi sig. They still have full control over whatever goes on

insights.claim: If PAPER became transferable, a perp market on PAPER would make attacks certain: an attacker could short PAPER and spend more on manipulating BTC/ETH than the house bankroll itself (team example: with a $10M bankroll a $15M attack loses money, but with $10M of PAPER short exposure a $15M attack becomes viable).
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Tradable tokens tied to a house pool create a reflexive short-and-attack loop; any similar casino token is structurally fragile.
insights.quote: It's not a matter of if that that will 100% happen if the token is made transferable, because anybody can whip up a perp market

insights.claim: A $10-15M Bitcoin trade is not large, so many actors, not just one or two, could execute such an attack once the pool grows big enough, which it likely would.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Attack economics scale with pool size: success of the protocol increases its own attack surface.

insights.claim: Mitigations exist (capping pool size, capping leverage) but they eliminate the reason to use PaperTrade, whose entire purpose is 1,000x degen gambling rather than 3x trading that users could do on Hyperliquid.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: The product's value proposition and its safety are in direct conflict, capping its long-run addressable size.
insights.quote: You're not going on Paper Trade to trade Bitcoin with 3x leverage the way you would on Hyperliquid

insights.claim: Roughly a week after launch, PaperTrade announced PAPER would no longer be made transferable 'at least for now', despite the roadmap listing transferability as a later phase; Pagalatis expects it won't be transferable for a long while, if ever.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Depositors who farmed losses for a token they expected to sell are holding a non-transferable claim; valuation assumptions collapse.
insights.quote: it seems pretty clear that they're not going to be transferable for a while, if not ever

insights.claim: The change is not a classic rug but a bait-and-switch: the team (described as very smart, including Blur and Jess) documented the oracle risk in advance and were likely aware of the second-order perp implication, yet still sold transferability to attract deposits.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the 'good communication' framing; reputational damage to the founders could weigh on future launches they back.
insights.quote: it's not exactly a rug in the sense that crypto Twitter is like very used to seeing

insights.claim: PaperTrade also changed its mint curve so each dollar lost now mints a fixed share of supply at that moment (roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost by Pagalatis' uncertain recollection), meaning losers no longer know what they receive in advance.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Tokenomics, yield, payback and transferability have all changed post-deposit; every participant needs to re-underwrite.

insights.claim: PaperTrade staking revenue fell from $2.1M on Sunday and $1.28M Monday to about $84.5K the next day (with 2 hours left), a 93% one-day drop, per a tweet cited on the show.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin
insights.so_what: The collapse reveals almost all volume was mercenary farming; organic demand for 1,000x leverage is a small fraction.

insights.claim: The post-announcement activity reveals true organic demand for 1,000x house-backed gambling, since farmers have no reason to keep losing money once PAPER cannot be sold; Pagalatis won't call it over but says recovery will be extremely tough and the opportunity cost of keeping capital there is too high.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Signals capital outflow from PaperTrade and caution on similar farm-driven HyperEVM launches.
insights.quote: what you now see is what the organic usage of people who want this type of thing is versus the activity that was there to potentially farm a token to then sell

insights.claim: Tokens work only when attached to a real business: treat a token like equity, which is valuable only if tied to a business with PMF, customers, retention and durability; most crypto tokens are speculative narratives instead.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Underwrite tokens on business fundamentals, not tokenomics engineering; token-as-product designs tend to fail.
insights.quote: if your token is the product, a lot of times it can't work

insights.claim: Hyperliquid is the model case of a token that works, because Hyperliquid was already successful before its token launched and would be successful without one.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Prefer protocols with pre-token product-market fit; the token is upside on an existing business.

insights.claim: MetaDAO's launchpad is a positive step for token launches because it vets projects more and has returned money to investors when ventures failed, rather than teams milking treasuries for years.
insights.speaker: Jason Pagalatis
insights.so_what: Launch venues with investor-protective mechanics (refunds on failure) may attract better-quality capital formation.
insights.quote: Return the money to investors like a like an ethical person would
